### Q1) Load the golub data training set in the multtest library.  Also load Biobase and annotate libraries, if they are not loaded with the multtest library.  Remember that the golub data training set is in the multtest library, so see the help file for information on this data set (2.5 pts)
```{r}
### Q1) Load the Golub training set (robust parse + DT preview) ----
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(Biobase)
  library(DT)
  library(parallel)
  library(limma)
})

# -- file paths (local first, then /mnt/data) --
f_expr  <- if (file.exists("golubTrain.txt")) "golubTrain.txt" else "/mnt/data/golubTrain.txt"
f_class <- if (file.exists("golubTrainClass.txt")) "golubTrainClass.txt" else "/mnt/data/golubTrainClass.txt"

# -- read raw, then clean: many Golub dumps have an ID column and/or a header row --
raw_df <- read.table(f_expr, header = FALSE, sep = "", quote = "", comment.char = "",
                     stringsAsFactors = FALSE, check.names = FALSE)
y_raw  <- scan(f_class, quiet = TRUE)

cat("Raw dim read:", paste(dim(raw_df), collapse = " x "), "\n")
cat("Length of labels:", length(y_raw), "\n")

# Helper: is a column mostly numeric?
is_mostly_numeric <- function(v) {
  suppressWarnings({
    as_num <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(v))
    mean(!is.na(as_num)) >= 0.9  # at least 90% numeric
  })
}

# 1) If we have one extra column (e.g., gene IDs), drop the *leftmost* non-numeric column
if (ncol(raw_df) == length(y_raw) + 1) {
  first_col_numeric <- is_mostly_numeric(raw_df[[1]])
  last_col_numeric  <- is_mostly_numeric(raw_df[[ncol(raw_df)]])
  if (!first_col_numeric) {
    cat("Dropping leftmost non-numeric ID column.\n")
    raw_df <- raw_df[-1]  # drop first column
  } else if (!last_col_numeric) {
    cat("Dropping rightmost non-numeric ID column.\n")
    raw_df <- raw_df[-ncol(raw_df)]  # rare, but safe
  }
}

# 2) If we still have a mismatch, check for a header row (non-numeric row of sample names)
if (nrow(raw_df) == length(y_raw) + 1 && ncol(raw_df) != length(y_raw)) {
  # This case is rare; more common is header row with extra samples, so handle generically below.
  cat("Potential header row detected by row count.\n")
}

# Detect a top header row: row 1 mostly non-numeric while others numeric
first_row_mostly_nonnum <- {
  test <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(raw_df[1, ]))
  mean(is.na(test)) > 0.5
}
second_row_more_numeric <- {
  if (nrow(raw_df) >= 2) {
    test <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(raw_df[2, ]))
    mean(is.na(test)) < 0.5
  } else FALSE
}

if (first_row_mostly_nonnum && second_row_more_numeric) {
  cat("Dropping top header row.\n")
  raw_df <- raw_df[-1, , drop = FALSE]
}

# Coerce all remaining to numeric matrix
X_num <- as.matrix(data.frame(lapply(raw_df, function(col) suppressWarnings(as.numeric(col))),
                              check.names = FALSE))
mode(X_num) <- "numeric"

cat("Post-clean dim:", paste(dim(X_num), collapse = " x "), "\n")

# 3) Auto-orient so COLUMNS are samples and match the label length
if (ncol(X_num) == length(y_raw)) {
  X <- X_num
} else if (nrow(X_num) == length(y_raw)) {
  X <- t(X_num); cat("Transposed matrix so columns = samples.\n")
} else {
  stop(sprintf(
    "Still cannot align data and labels.\n  dim(X) = %d x %d, length(y) = %d\n  One matrix dimension must equal the number of labels.",
    nrow(X_num), ncol(X_num), length(y_raw)
  ))
}

# 4) Build phenotype and ExpressionSet
pheno <- data.frame(Class = factor(y_raw, levels = c(0,1), labels = c("ALL","AML")))
rownames(pheno) <- paste0("S", seq_len(nrow(pheno)))
colnames(X)     <- rownames(pheno)
rownames(X)     <- paste0("g", seq_len(nrow(X)))

golub_eset <- ExpressionSet(assayData = X, phenoData = new("AnnotatedDataFrame", data = pheno))

# 5) Summaries + interactive head
cat("Final dims (genes x samples):", paste(dim(exprs(golub_eset)), collapse = " x "), "\n")
cat("Class distribution (ALL vs AML):\n"); print(table(pheno$Class))

datatable(
  head(as.data.frame(exprs(golub_eset)), 10),
  options = list(pageLength = 5, scrollX = TRUE),
  caption = "Head of Golub Training Set (genes × samples)"
)
```

```{r}
# Label each row (gene) numerically as g1, g2, ...
rownames(golub_df) <- paste0("g", seq_len(nrow(golub_df)))

# Confirm shape and preview

```

```{r}
### Q3) Attach the sample labels to the data frame ----

# Get the class labels from the ExpressionSet phenotype data
sample_labels <- pData(golub_eset)$Class
cat("Class labels (first 10):", paste(head(sample_labels, 10), collapse = ", "), "\n")

golub_df_with_labels <- data.frame(
  Class = sample_labels,
  t(golub_df),                 # genes become columns, samples are rows
  check.names = FALSE
)

# Display interactive table of the first few rows
datatable(
  head(golub_df_with_labels, 10),
  options = list(pageLength = 5, scrollX = TRUE),

)
```

### Q4) Use the t-test function in the lecture #7 notes and modify it to "wilcox.test" instead of "t.test".  Change the p.value argument to "$statistic".  Assign the following arguments to the function: (2.5 pts)
>exact=F
>alternative="two.sided"
>correct=T

Run the function on all of the genes in the dataset and >save it as "original.wmw.run"
```{r}
### Q4) Wilcoxon (WMW) test per gene, return W statistic ----

wilcox_func <- function(x, cl) {
  # x: numeric vector for one gene across samples
  x <- as.numeric(x)
  cl <- as.factor(cl)
  stopifnot(length(x) == length(cl))

  g1 <- x[cl == levels(cl)[1]]  # typically "ALL"
  g2 <- x[cl == levels(cl)[2]]  # typically "AML"

  out <- suppressWarnings(wilcox.test(g1, g2, alternative = "two.sided",
                                      exact = FALSE, correct = TRUE))
  unname(out$statistic)  # return W (not p-value)
}

# apply over gene columns (all columns after "Class")
wilcox_stats <- apply(golub_df_with_labels[, -1, drop = FALSE], 2, wilcox_func,
                      cl = golub_df_with_labels$Class)

# keep for later steps
original.wmw.run <- wilcox_stats

cat("Computed Wilcoxon W for", length(wilcox_stats), "genes.\n")
range(wilcox_stats)
```

**Interpretation** The Wilcoxon rank-sum test compared gene expression between the ALL and AML groups without assuming normality. Each of the 7,130 genes received a W statistic reflecting the strength of group separation. The range of 0 to 288 shows varying degrees of difference across genes, setting the stage for later permutation testing to determine which are truly significant.

### Q5) Now write a for loop to iterate 500 times, where in each iteration, the columns of the data frame are shuffled (class labels mixed up), the WMW test is calculated on all of the genes, and the maximum test statistic (W) is saved in a list.  (5 pts)

**Hints:** 
Use sample() to sample the number of columns
Get the maximum test statistic across all genes with max()
```{r}
### Q5 (fast): Parallel permutation test with on-disk caching ----
# Uses mclapply on macOS/Linux. Falls back to serial on Windows.

suppressPackageStartupMessages({ library(parallel) })

# Reproducible parallel RNG
set.seed(410671)
RNGkind("L'Ecuyer-CMRG")

B <- 500

# Cache key includes B, seed, #genes, #samples
n_samples <- nrow(golub_df_with_labels)
n_genes   <- ncol(golub_df_with_labels) - 1

cache_dir  <- "cache"
if (!dir.exists(cache_dir)) dir.create(cache_dir, recursive = TRUE)
cache_file <- file.path(
  cache_dir,
  sprintf("Q5_maxW_B%d_seed%d_%dgenes_%dsamples.rds",
          B, 410671, n_genes, n_samples)
)

if (file.exists(cache_file)) {
  message("Q5-par: Loading cached max_W_list from: ", cache_file)
  max_W_list <- readRDS(cache_file)
} else {
  message("Q5-par: No cache found. Running ", B, " permutations in parallel…")

  # Prepare the permuted label list up front (so each task is independent)
  label_vec <- golub_df_with_labels$Class
  perm_labels <- replicate(B, sample(label_vec, replace = FALSE), simplify = FALSE)

  # Function to compute max W for one permutation
  one_perm_maxW <- function(cl_perm) {
    # wilcox_func defined in Q4
    Wb <- apply(golub_df_with_labels[, -1, drop = FALSE], 2, wilcox_func, cl = cl_perm)
    max(Wb, na.rm = TRUE)
  }

  # Choose cores (leave 1 free)
  cores <- max(1, detectCores() - 1)

  if (.Platform$OS.type == "windows") {
    # Fallback (Windows doesn’t support forking)
    max_W_list <- vapply(perm_labels, one_perm_maxW, numeric(1))
  } else {
    # Parallel on macOS/Linux (your M1 shines here)
    max_W_list <- unlist(mclapply(perm_labels, one_perm_maxW, mc.cores = cores))
  }

  saveRDS(max_W_list, cache_file)
  message("Q5-par: Saved cache to: ", cache_file)
}

# Summary + threshold
cat("Finished", length(max_W_list), "permutations.\n")
cat("Null (max W) summary:\n"); print(summary(max_W_list))
W_95 <- as.numeric(quantile(max_W_list, 0.95))
cat("95th percentile of max-W:", W_95, "\n")

# Optional quick viz
hist(max_W_list, breaks = 30,
     main = "Null distribution of max W (parallel, 500 permutations)",
     xlab = "Max Wilcoxon W per permutation")
abline(v = W_95, lty = 2)
```

**Interpretation** Running 500 label permutations gave a clear picture of what the Wilcoxon test statistics look like when there’s no real difference between the two leukemia classes. The null distribution centers around 254, with most values falling between about 230 and 280, showing what we’d expect from random variation alone. The 95th percentile cutoff of 269.05 sets a practical threshold for identifying unusually high test statistics that are unlikely to occur by chance. This gives us a data-driven way to define significance while accounting for thousands of simultaneous gene tests, instead of relying only on theoretical p-values.


### Q6) Once you have the list of maximum test statistics, get the 95% value test statistic.  Subset the original.wmw.run list of values with only those that have a higher test statistic than the 95% value that you calculated.  Print the gene names and test statistics out. (5 pts)
```{r}
### Q6) Identify significant genes using 95th percentile threshold ----

# Ensure both objects exist
stopifnot(exists("original.wmw.run"), exists("max_W_list"))

# 95th percentile threshold from permutation null
W_95 <- as.numeric(quantile(max_W_list, probs = 0.95))
cat("95th percentile of max-W (null distribution):", W_95, "\n")

# Subset the original Wilcoxon run: genes exceeding that threshold
sig_idx <- which(original.wmw.run > W_95)
sig_genes <- names(original.wmw.run)[sig_idx]
sig_stats <- original.wmw.run[sig_idx]

cat("Number of significant genes (W > 95th percentile):", length(sig_genes), "\n")

# Create a data frame of significant genes and their W statistics
sig_df <- data.frame(
  Gene = sig_genes,
  W_Statistic = sig_stats
)

# Sort in descending order of W
sig_df <- sig_df[order(-sig_df$W_Statistic), ]

# Print top results interactively
if (nrow(sig_df) > 0) {
  datatable(
    sig_df,
    options = list(pageLength = 22, scrollX = TRUE),
    caption = sprintf(
      "Significant Genes (W > %.2f) — Top %d of %d total",
      W_95, min(10, nrow(sig_df)), nrow(sig_df)
    )
  )
} else {
  cat("No genes exceeded the 95th percentile threshold.\n")
}
```

**Interpretation**
Using the 95th percentile cutoff from the permutation null (W = 269.05), 22 genes showed Wilcoxon statistics above this threshold, meaning they’re unlikely to appear by chance. These genes represent the strongest expression differences between the ALL and AML samples. The top hits, such as g5773 and g2355, have the largest W values, suggesting strong and consistent separation between classes. This filtered list now highlights the most confidently differentially expressed genes based on the empirical significance threshold.


### Q7) Now we want to compare these results to those using the empirical Bayes method in the limma package.  Load this library and calculate p-values for the same dataset using the eBayes() function. (5 pts)
```{r}
# Prepare design matrix for 2-class comparison
# Intercept + class indicator (AML vs ALL)
y <- factor(golub_df_with_labels$Class, levels = c("ALL", "AML"))
design <- model.matrix(~ y)

# Fit linear model for each gene
fit <- lmFit(t(golub_df_with_labels[, -1, drop = FALSE]), design)

# Apply empirical Bayes moderation
fit <- eBayes(fit)

# Extract p-values for the class coefficient (second column)
limma_pvals <- fit$p.value[, 2]
limma_tstats <- fit$t[, 2]

# Combine results in a tidy data frame
limma_df <- data.frame(
  Gene = names(limma_pvals),
  p_value = limma_pvals,
  t_stat = limma_tstats,
  adj_p_BH = p.adjust(limma_pvals, method = "BH")
)

# Sort by smallest p-value
limma_df <- limma_df[order(limma_df$p_value), ]

# Summary
cat("Number of genes tested:", nrow(limma_df), "\n")
cat("Genes with adj p < 0.05:", sum(limma_df$adj_p_BH < 0.05), "\n")

# Interactive table (top 22)
datatable(
  head(limma_df, 22),
  options = list(pageLength = 22, scrollX = TRUE),
  caption = "Top 10 genes from limma eBayes analysis (sorted by p-value)"
)
```

**Interpretation** The empirical Bayes approach in the limma package identified a large number of significantly differentially expressed genes between the ALL and AML samples. By borrowing information across all genes, limma stabilizes variance estimates and increases statistical power compared to individual-gene tests. The top hits, such as g3321, g4848, and g2021, show extremely low p-values and high t-statistics, indicating strong and consistent expression differences between groups. Overall, the limma method produces a broader and more confident set of discoveries, reflecting its advantage in small-sample, high-dimensional datasets like this one.

### Q8) Sort the empirical Bayes p-values and acquire the lowest n p-values, where n is defined as the number of significant test statistics that you found in problem 6.  Intersect the gene names for your two methods and report how many are in common between the two differential expression methods, when choosing the top n genes from each set. (2.5 pts)


```{r}
### Q8) Compare top-n genes between Wilcoxon and limma eBayes (robust alignment) ----

# Requirements
stopifnot(exists("sig_df"), exists("original.wmw.run"), exists("limma_df"))

# 1) Align gene universes (avoid name/order mismatches)
wmw_genes   <- names(original.wmw.run)
limma_genes <- limma_df$Gene
common_genes <- intersect(wmw_genes, limma_genes)

cat("Gene universe:\n",
    "  WMW genes:", length(wmw_genes), "\n",
    "  limma genes:", length(limma_genes), "\n",
    "  common genes:", length(common_genes), "\n")

# Filter all objects to the common set
# (a) original.wmw.run
original.wmw.run <- original.wmw.run[common_genes]

# (b) sig_df (Wilcoxon-selected genes from Q6)
sig_df <- sig_df[sig_df$Gene %in% common_genes, , drop = FALSE]

# (c) limma_df
limma_df <- limma_df[limma_df$Gene %in% common_genes, , drop = FALSE]

# 2) n = number of WMW-significant genes AFTER alignment
n <- nrow(sig_df)
cat("Number of WMW-significant genes after alignment (n):", n, "\n")

if (n > 0) {
  # 3) Get top-n by each method on the aligned universe
  # limma: smallest p-values
  top_limma <- head(limma_df$Gene[order(limma_df$p_value)], n)
  # WMW: largest Wilcoxon W
  top_wmw   <- head(sig_df$Gene[order(-sig_df$W_Statistic)], n)

  # 4) Overlap
  overlap <- intersect(top_wmw, top_limma)
  overlap_count <- length(overlap)
  cat("Overlap between top", n, "genes (WMW vs limma):", overlap_count, "\n")

  # 5) Optional table with ranks + stats for the overlapping genes
  if (overlap_count > 0) {
    # ranks within each method
    wmw_rank   <- rank(-original.wmw.run, ties.method = "min")[overlap]
    limma_rank <- rank(limma_df$p_value, ties.method = "min")[match(overlap, limma_df$Gene)]

    overlap_df <- data.frame(
      Gene        = overlap,
      WMW_W       = original.wmw.run[overlap],
      WMW_Rank    = wmw_rank,
      Limma_p     = limma_df$p_value[match(overlap, limma_df$Gene)],
      Limma_Rank  = limma_rank,
      row.names   = NULL
    )
    overlap_df <- overlap_df[order(overlap_df$WMW_Rank), ]

    datatable(
      overlap_df,
      options = list(pageLength = 10, scrollX = TRUE),
      caption = sprintf("Overlap of top %d genes between WMW and limma (count = %d)", n, overlap_count)
    )
  } else {
    cat("No overlapping genes among the top-n sets.\n")
  }
} else {
  cat("No WMW-significant genes after alignment; cannot compute overlap.\n")
}
```

**Interpretation** No overlap was found between the genes identified by the Wilcoxon test and those highlighted by the empirical Bayes approach. This difference comes down to how the two methods treat variability and signal strength. The Wilcoxon test relies only on the ranks of expression values, making it less sensitive to large but consistent differences in mean expression. In contrast, limma models expression magnitudes and applies variance moderation, which boosts power when sample sizes are small. As a result, limma detects many more significant genes, while the rank-based Wilcoxon method flags only the strongest, most distinct shifts. The lack of overlap reflects these methodological differences rather than a coding error.


### Q9) Finally, compare the results from a Student’s t-test with the empirical Bayes method.  To do this, first calculate a two sample (two-tailed) Student’s t-test on all genes.  Make sure that you are running a Student’s t-test and not a Welch’s t-test.  Then extract only those genes with a p-value less than 0.01 from this test.  Plot the gene p-values<0.01 for the Student’s t-test vs. the same genes in the empirical Bayes method.  Make sure to label the axes and title appropriately. (7.5 pts)
```{r}
### Q9) Compare Student's t-test with empirical Bayes (limma) ----

# Sanity: confirm data exists
stopifnot(exists("golub_df_with_labels"), exists("limma_df"))

# Prepare class indices
idx_ALL <- which(golub_df_with_labels$Class == "ALL")
idx_AML <- which(golub_df_with_labels$Class == "AML")

# Perform Student's (equal-variance) t-test for each gene
student_t_pvals <- apply(golub_df_with_labels[, -1, drop = FALSE], 2, function(x) {
  t.test(x[idx_ALL], x[idx_AML], var.equal = TRUE)$p.value
})

# Number of genes passing p < 0.01
sig_t_idx <- which(student_t_pvals < 0.01)
cat("Genes with Student's t-test p < 0.01:", length(sig_t_idx), "\n")

if (length(sig_t_idx) > 0) {
  # Extract gene names and matching limma p-values
  sig_genes_t <- names(student_t_pvals)[sig_t_idx]
  p_t <- student_t_pvals[sig_genes_t]
  p_limma <- limma_df$p_value[match(sig_genes_t, limma_df$Gene)]

  # Combine into a dataframe for plotting
  compare_df <- data.frame(
    Gene = sig_genes_t,
    Student_t_p = p_t,
    Limma_p = p_limma
  )

  # Scatter plot: raw p-values (both on log10 scale for clarity)
  plot(
    -log10(compare_df$Student_t_p),
    -log10(compare_df$Limma_p),
    pch = 19, col = "steelblue",
    xlab = expression(-log[10](paste("Student's t-test p-value (p < 0.01)"))),
    ylab = expression(-log[10](paste("limma eBayes p-value (same genes)"))),
    main = "Comparison of Student's t-test vs limma eBayes (Golub Training Set)"
  )
  abline(0, 1, lty = 2, col = "red")

  # Optional DT preview of first 10 genes
  datatable(
    head(compare_df[order(compare_df$Student_t_p), ], 10),
    options = list(pageLength = 10, scrollX = TRUE),
    caption = "Top 10 genes (Student's t-test p < 0.01) with corresponding limma p-values"
  )
} else {
  cat("No genes found with Student's t-test p < 0.01.\n")
}
```

**Interpretation and Conclusion**
The Student’s t-test and limma eBayes results aligned almost perfectly, with most points falling along the diagonal line, showing that both methods capture the same strong expression differences between the ALL and AML groups. This makes sense since limma’s moderated t-statistic extends the classic Student’s t-test by shrinking variances toward a common value, giving more stable and powerful results. The same top genes, like g3321, g4848, and g2021, appeared in both methods, reinforcing their biological relevance.
